intro.opening: Karnak, Luxor Temple and the Luxor Museum: the three strongest reasons to spend a day on Luxor's east bank. Together they form the most coherent single-day argument for why the ancient Egyptians built the way they did. It's a private tour, operated for your party alone.
intro.whyThisOrder: Luxor in summer is brutally hot by mid-morning, so the tour begins early, and the day opens at Karnak, because no other site in Egypt prepares you for quite what this complex turns out to be. The afternoon concludes at the Luxor Museum. Because the day is yours, the order and the dwell times bend to your party: more temple, less museum, or the reverse.
intro.returnNote: You finish in time to spend the evening on your own terms.

intro.closingLine: Karnak, Luxor Temple, and the museum between them contain a larger proportion of surviving ancient Egyptian history than any other single day's itinerary can offer.

stops.title: The Karnak complex
stops.text: Closer to a religious city than a temple, built up across roughly 1,500 years. You enter the Precinct of Amun-Ra through pylons that increase in age as you move inward, into the Great Hypostyle Hall: 134 sandstone columns in 16 rows, the central ones nearly 21 metres tall. Beyond are the obelisks of Thutmose I and Hatshepsut, the sacred lake and the Festival Temple of Thutmose III.

stops.title: Along the Avenue of Sphinxes
stops.text: From Karnak, the tour moves south along the Avenue of Sphinxes, the 2.7-kilometre processional road connecting the two great temples of ancient Thebes. Ram-headed sphinxes line the Karnak end, human-headed sphinxes the Luxor Temple end.

stops.title: Luxor Temple
stops.text: Raised by Amenhotep III and added to by Ramses II, whose pylon carries scenes from the Battle of Kadesh. One of its two obelisks still stands; the other has been in the Place de la Concorde in Paris since 1836. The mosque of Abu Haggag sits in the northeast corner: the temple never fully disappeared from use.

stops.title: The Luxor Museum
stops.text: A small, exceptionally well-curated museum on the Corniche, concentrating on New Kingdom material from Thebes. Highlights include the reconstructed Akhenaten wall from a dismantled Aten temple at Karnak, the statuary cache found beneath the Luxor Temple courtyard in 1989, and military equipment and chariots from the reigns of Ahmose I and Thutmose III.

stops.title: End of the day
stops.text: You finish in time to spend the evening on your own terms.
